newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's "Rambo" policeman says he was provoked.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's "Rambo" policeman says he was provoked.

text.p: A Sao Paulo military police officer accused of killing a civilian in a videotaped incident that has shocked Brazil defended police violence by saying the officers were provoked, newspapers said on Saturday.
"If we overdid it, it's because we were provoked," daily newspaper Estado de Sao Paulo quoted the officer as telling a judge investigating accusations against 10 military police officers.
The men were filmed torturing and intimidating civilians at a roadblock they set up in a shantytown in suburban Sao Paulo.
The footage, aired on Brazilian television 12 days ago, was condemned by human rights groups who said police brutality was endemic in Brazil but that officers were rarely punished.

The video, which has been shown repeatedly on several channels, has triggered a wave of public outcry against police abuses. Dozens of people have shared tales of humiliating experiences at the hands of officers.

Officer Otavio Lourenco Gambra, nicknamed "Rambo" by the Brazilian media, has been fingered as the man who allegedly fired a shot at a car which hit a passenger. The man, Mario Jose Josino, later died in a hospital.
Gambra admitted on Friday to firing a shot near the car as it was slowly driving away, but said he aimed at the floor, not the inside of the vehicle.
"I am fully confident that my shot did not hit anyone, only the floor," Estado de Sao Paulo quoted him as saying.
He also said: "That citizen who was in the (car) already had his days numbered, and even if we hadn't fired a shot, he would have shown up dead a few days later."
Gambra defended techniques used by the police officers, who were shown in the video slapping civilians, beating them on the back and hitting one man repeatedly on the soles of his feet.

"We had orders to act energetically and without violence in the shantytown. If there had been violence, there would have been broken arms and other fractures," he was quoted as saying in the daily Folha de Sao Paulo.
He blamed low salaries and the pressures of the job for desensitizing military police officers.
Nine of the officers have denied accusations including beating, extortion and murder. One has admitted to hitting a young man in the face, saying he was responding to insults.
The court expects to sentence the officers before the end of the year. A separate military police disciplinary committee has been set up to deal with the incident.
